Open-source embedded engineering workbench

Firmware should
prove itself.

Embeder turns a firmware goal into grounded source, compiles it with a real ARM toolchain, boots it in Renode, and records the evidence. The model drafts. Deterministic oracles decide.

Closed-loop by design

The LLM never certifies its own output.

Every draft crosses a verifiability boundary. Compiler diagnostics can drive a bounded repair loop; only a successful build and simulation promote the result to verified.

01 / Grounding

Datasheet facts, not guesses

Register addresses come from bundled CMSIS-SVD data and travel with source citations.

USART2.CR10x4000440C sourcestm32f4-mini.svd
02 / Build

Real compiler diagnostics

Embeder invokes the ARM GNU toolchain and maps errors back into the editable workspace.

BUILD ✓ firmware.elf · Cortex-M4
03 / Evidence

Simulation closes the loop

Renode boots the ELF, observes USART2, and records what was—and was not—verified.

UART ✓ Hello from Embeder

Documentation

From installer to verified firmware.

The desktop shell installs in one pass. Add the compiler and simulator when you are ready to run the real verification path.

01

Install Embeder

Download the current Windows x64 setup from the official GitHub release and run it. Embeder installs for the current user and creates a sandboxed starter workspace on first launch.

Release integrity

Verify the installer before running it if your browser marks the unsigned community build as unfamiliar.

SHA-256 6E1CBEF44BEF8DAC29F943E31A77E72E7AFFAEECBFF452EE9FC1067323858540
Open the latest release ↗
02

Add the verification toolchain

The editor and grounded datasheet views work immediately. The real build path expects the following developer tools:

Arm GNU ToolchainRequired for Buildarm-none-eabi-gcc ↗ RenodeRequired for Build & Simulate1.16.x ↗ Python 3Optional for model-backed generation3.12+ ↗

Validated baseline: Arm GNU 12.2.1 and Renode 1.16.x. Newer versions should be treated as unverified until the real integration suite passes.

03

Run your first closed loop

  1. 1

    Open the bundled stm32-blink-uart workspace.

  2. 2

    Edit and save src/main.c.

  3. 3

    Choose Build for a real ELF, or Build & Simulate for the UART assertion.

  4. 4

    Inspect diagnostics, evidence, citations and the verifiability boundary.

04

Bring your own model

Embeder auto-detects a supported provider from the environment. With no key, generation falls back to deterministic grounded synthesis.

PowerShell
$env:GEMINI_API_KEY = "..."
# or
$env:OPENAI_API_KEY = "..."
# or
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = "..."

Keys stay local to the process. Generated drafts remain proposals until the deterministic build and simulation stages pass.

05

Build from source

Contributors need Git, Rust with the MSVC target, Visual Studio C++ Build Tools, and Tauri CLI v2.

PowerShell
git clone https://github.com/pksark06-beep/Embeder.git
cd Embeder

rustup toolchain install stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
cargo install tauri-cli --version "^2" --locked
cargo test --workspace

cd desktop/src-tauri
cargo +stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc tauri build \
  --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
06

Architecture

The renderer never decides verification state. A shared Rust API owns workspace access and launches short-lived, path-jailed MCP workers over stdio JSON-RPC.

PresentationTauri workbenchHTML · CSS · JavaScript
↓ invoke
ApplicationShared Rust APITasks · workspace · evidence
↓ stdio MCP
WorkerDatasheetCMSIS-SVD
WorkerFirmwareARM GCC
WorkerSimulationRenode
07

Security model

  • Workspace file access is restricted to the seeded firmware project.
  • Generated builds run in unique temporary directories.
  • MCP workers expose a fixed tool catalog and reject traversal.
  • Model output cannot mark itself verified.
  • Process isolation is application-level, not an operating-system sandbox.
